content: Migraine is a common neurologic disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of moderate to severe headache, typically affecting one side of the head and often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound (photophobia and phonophobia). Migraines can vary between individuals and may last from a few hours up to 72 hours. The underlying mechanisms involve complex interactions of neuronal hyperexcitability, cortical spreading depression, and activation of the trigeminovascular system which leads to headache pain and associated symptoms. Genetics also play a significant role as migraines tend to run in families. Trigger factors include hormonal changes, stress, certain foods, sleep disturbances, and environmental stimuli. Evaluation of migraine relies on clinical history and symptom description, as there is no definitive laboratory or imaging test. Effective management includes acute treatments to relieve pain during attacks and preventive therapies aimed at reducing frequency and severity. Pharmacologic options include analgesics, triptans, antiemetics, and various preventive medications such as beta-blockers and anticonvulsants. Non-pharmacologic approaches like lifestyle modifications, regular sleep, stress management, and avoiding known triggers are important for many patients. Awareness of red flags is crucial to rule out secondary causes of headaches. Limitations include variable individual responses to treatments and incomplete understanding of migraine pathophysiology. Safety considerations involve monitoring side effects of medications and recognizing when urgent evaluation is needed, such as sudden severe headaches or neurological changes. Major synonyms and related terms include "vascular headache" (older terminology), "hemicrania," and "migraine headache." This module provides a comprehensive overview to empower patients and caregivers in understanding and managing migraine effectively, while highlighting current scientific knowledge and clinical practices.

content: Migraine is a chronic neurologic condition typified by recurrent headaches of moderate to severe intensity. There are several recognized types, including migraine without aura (common migraine) and migraine with aura, which involves transient neurological symptoms such as visual disturbances preceding the headache phase. Other subtypes include chronic migraine, characterized by headaches occurring 15 or more days per month. Understanding these types assists in diagnosis and tailored management.

content: Migraine involves complex pathophysiological processes including neuronal hyperexcitability and cortical spreading depression—a wave of neuronal and glial depolarization across the cerebral cortex—which likely triggers activation of the trigeminal nerve and release of vasoactive neuropeptides causing inflammation and pain. Genetic predisposition affects neuronal ion channels and neurotransmitter pathways. The trigeminovascular system plays a key role in headache pain generation. Research continues to clarify molecular and neurochemical underpinnings.

content: Risk factors for migraine include family history, hormonal changes (notably in women during menstruation), stress, sleep disturbances, certain foods and beverages (e.g., caffeine, alcohol), and environmental factors. Migraine exhibits a strong genetic component, with heritability estimates around 40-60%. Studies have identified several gene variants linked to familial hemiplegic migraine and common migraine, though gene-environment interactions are important.

content: Migraine commonly presents with a unilateral, pulsatile headache lasting 4 to 72 hours, often aggravated by physical activity. Associated symptoms typically include nausea, vomiting, photophobia (light sensitivity), and phonophobia (sound sensitivity). Aura symptoms, when present, include visual disturbances such as flashing lights or blind spots, sensory changes, or speech difficulties. Prodromal and postdromal symptoms can include mood changes, neck stiffness, and fatigue.

content: Migraine diagnosis is clinical, based on history and symptom pattern fitting International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD) criteria. There are no definitive laboratory or imaging tests for migraine, but brain imaging may be used to exclude secondary causes in atypical presentations. A thorough neurological exam is essential. Patient headache diaries may assist in diagnosis and treatment planning.

content: Acute migraine therapies aim to relieve pain and associated symptoms during an attack. Options include over-the-counter analgesics like acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), as well as prescription triptans targeting serotonin receptors to constrict blood vessels and inhibit pain pathways. Antiemetics may be used for nausea. Early treatment upon migraine onset improves effectiveness. Caution with medication overuse which can lead to rebound headaches.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: For frequent or severe migraines, preventive medications may reduce attack frequency and severity. Common preventives include beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol), calcium channel blockers, anticonvulsants (e.g., topiramate), and antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline). Newer treatments include monoclonal antibodies targeting calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP). Lifestyle measures complement pharmacologic approaches. Preventive therapy requires time to assess efficacy and patient monitoring for side effects.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Lifestyle modifications are foundational to migraine management. Regular sleep patterns, hydration, balanced diet, avoidance of triggers, stress reduction techniques, and regular aerobic exercise can decrease migraine frequency and severity. Behavioral therapies such as cognitive-behavioral therapy and biofeedback may help. Identifying personal triggers through headache diaries supports avoidance strategies. These approaches have minimal side effects and improve overall wellbeing.

chunk_title: Safety and When to Seek Urgent Care
content: While migraines are generally benign, certain symptoms warrant urgent evaluation such as sudden severe headache unlike previous headaches ('thunderclap'), neurological deficits, seizures, fever with neck stiffness, or changes in consciousness. Some medications for migraine can have contraindications or adverse effects; consultation with a healthcare provider is critical. Awareness of medication overuse headache is important for safe treatment practices.

content: Misconceptions include the belief that migraines are 'just bad headaches' or purely psychological. Migraine is a complex neurological disorder with identifiable pathophysiology. Another misconception is that caffeine is always harmful; while it can trigger in some, it may relieve headaches in others. Some believe that migraines always have aura, but most cases do not. Education helps reduce stigma and improve treatment adherence.
